lead:
The research map was built from **one collection** — *Croatia, Church Books, 1516–1994* — and its standfirst claimed to show *«every parish in Croatia whose registers are on film»*. It never did.

So on **15 September 2026** the whole of FamilySearch was walked: **all 3,488 historical record collections**, every title read, and **every one that could plausibly hold a record for this family's ground opened through its browse tree or searched inside**.

**This page is the complete result, including the failures.** A negative is recorded as carefully as a find, because the point of it is that nobody has to walk that collection again.

findings.text:
**Five collections hold places on this family's ground, and all five are now on the map.**

*Croatia, Church Books* (the original) · *Croatia, Delnice Deanery* — a second Croatian collection nobody knew was there, browsable only by film · *Italy, Pola and Trieste* — five Croatian Istrian parishes filed by Italy · *Slovenia, Prekmurje and Međimurje* — **46 districts, nearly all Croatian towns, under Hungarian names** · and *Italy, Udine*, already here for Carnia.

**Thirty-nine others were opened and hold nothing for us.**

findings.lab: What is not there at all
findings.text:
**There is no Serbian, Bosnian, Montenegrin or Yugoslav collection in FamilySearch.** Not one, in 3,488. The Dalmatian hinterland has no coverage from that direction.

**And Croatia itself has exactly two collections.** For a country with a thousand-year parish record, that is the whole of it.

findings.lab: Why Austria and Hungary both failed, which is the useful part
findings.text:
Both looked like the obvious hiding place for **Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan** — the three parishes at the centre of this family that the Croatian collection does not hold. Both came back empty, and between them they explain why.

**Hungary introduced civil registration in 1895; Croatia-Slavonia did not**, keeping the parish books as the legal record until **1946**. So there is no Croatian civil registration anywhere to find — it was never created. And **Austria's collection is a name index of the Alpine dioceses**, not of the Littoral, which stopped being Austrian in 1918 and whose registers stayed in Istria.

**On present evidence those three parishes are filmed nowhere at all.** [Pazin holds the paper](/undigitised/), and that is the only route left.

findings.lab: And a warning the walk handed over for free
findings.text:
**Defranceschi is not a rare name. It is a Veneto name.**

**9,626** records at Padova · **6,546** at Venice · **2,076** at Verona · **1,285** at Treviso · **289** in Tyrol, around Bozen and Salorno.

None of them is this family, and none can be shown not to be without a document. The [Mione households](/carnia/) already proved the surname was a population rather than a family in one valley. **This is the same proof at the scale of a province**, and it is why this archive will not bridge two places on a name.

close:
**The method is the part worth keeping.** `/platform/records/collections/<cc>/waypoints` opens the browse tree of **any** FamilySearch collection, and `f.collectionId` on the persona search counts names inside one. Between them a candidate is answered in two calls — which is how thirty-four of them were cleared in an evening.

*The filter was verified rather than trusted*: the same surname returns **303,320** unfiltered, **289** in Austria, **3,550** in Croatia, and **0** against a made-up collection id.
